entries.title: Wikipedians Believed AI Would Come and Go. They Were Wrong
entries.summary: In a world of AI Overviews, Wikipedia usage declines. But the real loss may be far more existential than website traffic.
entries.content:
Long before the storm of AI struck Wikipedia, the Wikimedia Foundation was making preparations. Wikipedians battened down the hatches and made confident-sounding predictions that it would break and wash over them. Large language models might even improve Wikipedia, it was said, automating more of the housekeeping—formatting, sources, citations, missing links—and so freeing up humans to do creative work. It was not so simple. In 2019, then-Wikimedia Foundation head Katherine Maher wrote an op-ed in The New York Times under the headline “Without Humans, A.I. Can Wreak Havoc.” “Too often,” she wrote, “artificial intelligence is presented as an all-powerful solution to our problems, a scalable replacement for people.” The issue confronting Wikipedia, retaining human control over machines, was the same one soon being faced everywhere.

Already in 2018 Google was training AI to write “Wikipedia-like articles,” and by October 2024, a Princeton University study found that about 5 percent of nearly 3,000 newly created articles on English Wikipedia in a single month (August 2024) contained a substantial amount of AI-generated content. There were signs. ChatGPT was fond of em dashes—parenthetical statements that look like this one—and curly quotation marks. Sometimes, residues from the prompts used to compose articles were left behind (“Here is your Wikipedia article,” they might say.)

At first, Wikipedians tried to shape and control AI, to make its output “acceptable and constructive,” or to fix or remove if it proved otherwise. Generic fluff like “praising a village for its fertile farmlands, livestock, and scenic countryside” and fake sources were weeded out. By March 2026, AI content was found to violate its core principles so often that writing with large language models was banned outright, and their role restricted to translation and minor proofreading.

A much-read essay titled “Death of Wikipedia” explained this defensive posture. It predicted a ripple effect: As contributors reduced their contributions in response to AI pervading the platform, there might be a temptation to replace their work with still more AI, creating a downward spiral. One viral X post lamented that artificial intelligence seemed to be changing things in the wrong direction: “I want AI to do my laundry and dishes so that I can do art and writing, not for AI to do my art and writing so that I can do my laundry and dishes.” The “Death of Wikipedia” warned against something similar: Rather than AI performing Wikipedia’s “housekeeping” roles, it might compose its articles instead, leaving humans relegated to formatting and cleanup. The result would trap editors in an endless curatorial project derived not from human priorities but from the frostbitten harvests of machines.

“The potential ‘whittling down’ each year of our pool of talented writers is the greatest threat to Wikipedia,” another Wikipedian wrote, “as we must increase the number of editors, especially expert editors, to be able to fix the sprawling hellscape of weak, inaccurate and incomplete articles that drag down the project.” A Wikipedia written and read by machines threatened to create a new, deracinated Wikipedia, stripped not only of its context, but of its animating passion. It would be artless, and soulless. When the Wikimedia Foundation says that the care and commitment of Wikipedians to “reliable encyclopedic knowledge is something AI cannot replace,” that is not the same as saying that it will not be replaced.

Once Google introduced AI Overviews in search, they quickly became as central to the experience as Wikipedia was until recently. (This also means Wikipedia still does play a crucial role as a source, only at one step removed.) Anyone who uses AI agents knows that they give plausible, almost intuitive answers, which can pass a superficial review of their sourcing. They are also often wrong. If Wikipedia itself becomes corrupted by artificial intelligence, by what means will we prove when they are wrong?

Implicit in the idea of a single, machine-edited encyclopedia to rule them all is that such a phenomenon should act as a final authority. Its appeal, to the kind of people who find it appealing, is that it will be coolly rational, a kind of digital King Solomon that can act as a disinterested arbiter. There is no reason to think such cold logic would not be cruel instead. Its aesthetic failings are a clue: “Slop” is a useful word for the product of artificial intelligence, which implies something unvariegated and monotonous, absent not only of nutritional value but also of the flavor that makes nutrition a pleasure.

There is also no reason to believe an AI encyclopedia, or any other encyclopedia, should be unifying. Whatever its shortcomings and eccentricities, Wikipedia is the closest thing to an “encyclopedia of everything” we have ever had. Once smartphones became widespread after the iPhone’s launch in 2007, the old speculations, however far-reaching, were realized: Wikipedia was costless, portable, immediate, and electric. Enormous and omnipresent, it really became an approximation of the “sum of all human knowledge.” But so what? What did access to this oracle mean for human flourishing? What good has Wikipedia done?

A documentary maker, wanting to bring Wikipedia’s story to the screen, asked me a sharpened version of this question. Yes, Wikipedia was the little encyclopedia that could. It had overcome humble origins to become massive. But the dictates of streaming television needed something more. Were there, she asked, any real-life episodes where Wikipedia had “saved the village”? Has Wikipedia saved lives? The answer is “probably,” though not in dramatic or famous ways. Quick-fire encyclopedic knowledge has helped with accidental poisoning, and there are signs that Wikipedia is accessed with special frequency during natural disasters. But these anecdotes are difficult to corroborate, and often, when Wikipedia’s role is scrutinized, it turns out to be incidental. If someone calls for help in an emergency, it is not the phone which is the hero.

Does Wikipedia perform a public good? This seems self-evident but is much harder to measure and, in a way, is out of the project’s hands. In 2013, when an online poster posed the question “If someone from the 1950s suddenly appeared today, what would be the most difficult thing to explain to them about life today?” the top answer went viral as a mordant sign of the times: “I possess a device, in my pocket, that is capable of accessing the entirety of information known to man. I use it to look at pictures of cats and get in arguments with strangers.” Elsewhere, the “arguments with strangers” line was expressed in less lighthearted ways. “The greatest threat to democracy may no longer derive from human agency but from new forms of technology, which have the capacity to undermine democracy without anyone having intended it,” the academic David Runciman wrote two years later. “The forces from which democracy needs rescuing are no longer pressing on it from the outside. They come from within.”

No one is credited with foreseeing Wikipedia more clearly than H. G. Wells, a reputation built on a series of essays collected in his book World Brain, and its advocacy for a “Permanent World Encyclopaedia.” But Wells expounded on this idea many times, and his other writings were much more equivocal, and he even satirized his own obsessions in The Camford Visitation: “He wants a universally educated world, educated on the same lines, with every artificial difference eliminated. He is a cantankerous, disagreeable little nobody and yet at times one feels he has got hold of something most exasperatingly vast and right.” Soon after World Brain was published, Wells had lost faith in his encyclopedic vision altogether and succumbed to late-life pessimism. Humanity had orchestrated to create a world war, not a world brain, and in the civilizational race between “education and catastrophe,” as he put it, catastrophe looked to have a winning lead.

Less obvious to us now is that World Brain was also an antidote. The most significant new European encyclopedias that preceded it, the Great Soviet Encyclopedia and the Enciclopedia Italiana, were direct expressions of nationalist and totalitarian intent, so much so that the entry on “Fascism” in the Enciclopedia Italiana was credited to Benito Mussolini himself. Wells understood that “internationalism” needed its own encyclopedia as a counterweight, but that did not make it a simple force for freedom. He assumed that the World Brain would assist a world government in projecting its power, and though democratically available, his Permanent World Encyclopaedia would make such a world government omnipotent. A world government that was all-seeing as well as all-knowing would inevitably be repressive; a sinister side to Wells’ ideas seemed to have partly inspired George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four.

Orwell also critiqued Wells more explicitly in his 1941 essay “Wells, Hitler, and the World State.” One of its more perceptive observations is that Wells was not, in fact, a futurist. He was a nostalgic, Orwell thought, a “nineteenth-century liberal” who had spent 40 years repeating the same idea: that history was a battle between “the man of science who is working towards a planned World State” and “the reactionary who is trying to restore a disorderly past.” With Orwell’s help, we can see that Wells’ World Brain was an old idea, not a new one. Versions of it had preexisted Wells by centuries, and this particular encyclopedic worldview sprang from his Edwardian conception of Progress with a capital P.

The encyclopedia handed down to us from the Enlightenment is much more than a collation of facts in a book or on a website. It is a whole mode of seeing and doing, a lens through which a clear, scientific vision of all things can come into view, unobstructed by superstition. Witness the world in this way, and the world changes. So far-reaching is this idea that the philosopher Alasdair MacIntyre classed “encyclopaedia” as one of the three major approaches of Western ethics, what he called “rival versions of moral enquiry.” The others were “tradition,” starting with Thomas Aquinas and Aristotle, and “genealogy,” which began with Nietzsche. Tradition was a marriage of faith and reason. Genealogy emphasized hidden power relations. Encyclopaedia relied on reason alone, trying to build an objective picture of the world that could determine how to act, thanks to a consensus version of the truth. The purest expression of this was to be found in the 19th century, in the ninth edition of Encyclopaedia Britannica, which promised “the available facts of human history, collected over the widest areas … carefully coordinated and grouped together, in the hope of ultimately evolving the laws of progress, moral and material, which underlie them.”

When Three Rival Versions of Moral Enquiry was published in 1990, MacIntyre’s notion was already criticized for being out of date. One reviewer complained that it saddled “the encyclopaedists with their 19th-century dogmatic statements in Britannica and plays down the fact that few if any of their heirs hold such views today.” Yet there were some places that rational-liberal outlook did survive in an unapologetic form. It remained at the very forefront of Encyclopaedia Britannica—the 1987 edition opened with the motto of its associate, the University of Chicago: “Let knowledge grow from more to more and thus be human life enriched.” Most pertinently, it undergirded the beliefs of Wikipedia’s cofounders. Not only did Wikipedia’s text-heavy format reflect a centuries-old Enlightenment tradition, it was also created by two men who still believed, earnestly, that discovering the facts and learning lessons from them was not only the purpose of an encyclopedia, but the central task of a life well lived.

The divergent paths of Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger offer a kind of parable for the fate of this worldview and the cultural crosscurrents that swamped it. Twenty-five years after Wikipedia’s founding, Wales is still a Davos Man, an international person for an international project, who lives in the capital of the United Kingdom and makes frequent criticism of the MAGA movement. Sanger never left Ohio, where he homeschooled his children, became a vocal vaccine skeptic during the Covid-19 pandemic, and voted for Donald Trump. In 2025, he announced that he had given up his long-standing agnosticism to become a professing Christian, and wrote a book-length philosophical proof for the existence of God. If Wales remained wedded to the MacIntyre-style notion of “encyclopedia”—Enlightenment rationalism, with an added Objectivist trim—Sanger had returned to “tradition.”

As Wikipedia affirmed its status as a knowledge institution, it also lost its immunity from the crises afflicting knowledge institutions everywhere. The only surprise was that it had been exempt for so long. At the end of her tenure as head of the Wikimedia Foundation, Sue Gardner had likened the experience to living on a peaceful tropical island as “cruise missiles flew overhead.” Culture war had broken out all around, and now Wikipedia was an island no more. In the 2010s, “disinformation,” “misinformation,” and “fake news” were all selected as words of the year in short order, and the saturation of information was just as blameworthy as its corruption. Instead of adjudicating between facts like judges, audiences acted like lawyers assembling a brief and took only what they wanted. The results of “doing your own research,” an off-kilter version of the Enlightenment demand “dare to know,” were algorithmically personalized pseudo-informational systems. Mired in this uncertain environment, Wikipedia approached its 25th anniversary facing unprecedented political, cultural, and technological threats.

All of this added an elegiac note to its birthday celebrations in January 2026. The Pew Research company marked the occasion by quantifying the encyclopedia’s staggering reach—in the decade between 2015 and 2025, Wikipedia had been viewed 1.9 trillion times, an average of 508 million views per day. These immense numbers nevertheless contained an unmistakable arc of decline. In the days prior to the anniversary, a long-time Wikipedian, Christophe Henner, published a long and detailed “wake-up call” for the Wikipedia movement. Since 2022, the encyclopedia had lost almost a quarter of its readership, more than 1.1 billion visits per month, a missing audience who, presumably, were seeking out AI summaries instead. Even when answers offered by AI agents contain links, readers tend not to follow them: One figure showed that the click-through rate from AI chatbots was only 0.33 percent; for the Google search engine, it had been closer to 9 percent. For a model whose lifeblood was readers becoming editors, it was a disaster.

Artificial intelligence was an existential risk to Wikipedia, Henner warned, and the encyclopedia risked being remembered as a “historical artifact that AI once trained on … a footnote in the training data of models that have moved on without us.” An editing crisis meant that fewer and fewer editors were performing more and more labor, “a smaller club working harder to maintain something fewer people see,” as he put it. Past moments of opportunity—for example, when Wikipedia might have harnessed the growth of the internet outside Western countries—had mostly been squandered. The energy generated by places like India and Nigeria going digital had passed Wikipedia by, and in the wake of all this, the encyclopedia risked becoming a “temple,” maintained by the last in a priest class of superannuated Wikipedians. Once sacrilegious ideas, like paying editors for their work, had to be considered anew. Otherwise, the whole of Wikipedia might be reduced to an abandoned cathedral.

Media coverage marking the occasion was just as bittersweet. In Nature, Dariusz Jemielniak wrote that “academic indifference” and artificial intelligence threatened Wikipedia’s survival, accusing agentic AI of exploiting a “parasitic relationship” that “endangers the last bastion of freely accessible, human-curated knowledge and undermines the premise of collaboration on which many of Wikipedia’s knowledge-sharing practices rely.” “Wikipedia’s Existential Threats Feel Greater Than Ever” was the headline for a Stephen Harrison piece in WIRED, a catalog of threats beleaguering the project. More dangerous than hostile think tanks and lawmakers was an increasingly indifferent public, slowly drifting away from its founding ideals. “Economic precarity [has] trained many Gen Zers to see any unpaid labor as a scam,” Harrison wrote. In the cold light of the dawning era, becoming a Wikipedia super editor during a period of unemployment seemed a distant luxury, or outright perplexing, “thankless work that AI companies strip-mine for a profit.”

The tide turning on Wikipedia was more than the advent of artificial intelligence or a fragmentation of reading habits. Christophe Henner thought the “AI summaries” were only a “convenient explanation.” “I’m skeptical,” he wrote:

Even this undersold the quantum of change. Something far older was fast losing relevance as well: It was the beginning of the end of the encyclopedic age. Near the front of the French Encyclopédie there is a diagram called the “figurative system of human knowledge,” which is now sometimes called “The Tree of Diderot and d’Alembert.” The Tree is a system for not only ordering “the parts of knowledge,” but connecting them in a logical chain so long it can wreath the universe. It represents a bold idea: that an encyclopedia’s unifying force will show how everything in existence is linked. It suggests that knowing everything will lead to knowing One Big Thing about everything. This old-fashioned idea was resuscitated in the computer age, and gathered momentum with the concept of AGI, artificial general intelligence, the moment machines surpass every form of human understanding. If realized, it will represent not only the end of encyclopedias, but their culmination. Human-written encyclopedias will still exist after AGI, but only as secular scriptures in the mind of a digital god.

The longest-standing critique of “encyclopaedia” is religious: It is the belief that human activity on a godlike scale is a doomed act of conceit. It was only during the Enlightenment that absolute knowledge came to be considered beneficial (and today, “know-it-all” is still an insult, not a compliment). Beforehand, desire for absolute knowledge was viewed as a sin or a crime, a proscription that continues in many cultures. Greek mythology is full of cautionary figures like Pandora and Prometheus, who knew too much and suffered for it; when the Norse god Odin seeks the sacred well waters granting wit and wisdom, a single drink costs him one of his eyes. In the very first book of the Bible, two different stories, the Tower of Babel and the Garden of Eden, carry variations on the same moral: Total understanding must be God’s alone. Curiosity is not only a sin, but the first sin.

One of the many artworks inspired by Wikipedia speaks to this phenomenon. In the 2010s, the bio-artist Joe Davis declared that he would engineer a real, living Tree of Knowledge, the tree described in the Bible that holds forbidden fruit and results in the fall of humankind. To do so, Davis planned to take a 4,000-year-old strain of apple trees and copy the English-language edition of Wikipedia into the letters of its DNA. He called the project Malus ecclesia, which in Latin is a pun that means both “evil church” and “apple tree church.” In interviews, Davis refused to say whether he would eat the Tree’s fruit; because of laws around genetic modification, ingesting an apple or even planning to may have been a criminal act. Mired in red tape, this tantalizing idea never came to fruition, but its forbidding message remains: The sum of all knowledge is cursed.

The real existing Wikipedia feels less melodramatic than that, and the most lasting dividend of Wikipedia may not be its contents but its process, which holds a promise quite unlike the Tree of Knowledge or even the Tree of Diderot. For years, the annual Wikimania conference has sustained a fledgling tradition: At the opening ceremony, Wikipedians wear their national dress. When almost three-quarters of the nations on earth are in attendance, this produces a real spectacle, even against a backdrop of convention center carpet. All around the room are people wearing hanboks and kaftans and kimonos (the practice was initiated by a Japanese Wikipedian), and when they intermingle, the effect is like those old, quaintly hopeful pictures canvassing the “Peoples of the World.” Appreciating the depth and variety on display takes longer. Those golden headdresses, called serimpak, are worn by the seafaring tribes of Borneo, and that is why they are shaped like ships. The chapan robes that seem to swirl under their resplendent colors are from central Asia; those heavy ponchos, overkill against the air-conditioning, have come all the way from the Andes. Someone offers Jimmy Wales a conical nomad’s hat from Burkina Faso, but he cannot accept all the paraphernalia presented to him. There is too much.

Those might be lederhosen in the distance, although someone jokes that the real German national dress is sandals with socks. At least one tech type seems to be wearing Hawaiian shorts for a similar reason, as the official livery of Silicon Valley. Everywhere there is embroidery, silk and brocaded colors, headscarves and skullcaps, a pageant of signs and patterns from parts unknown. Once congregated, the people wearing this garb do not generate an atmosphere of hubris. In this room their shared mission seems humble. Their talk is the slow, uncertain work of mutual understanding, graced with the tentative socializing of the shy. They are bounded by human fallibility, the same thing that ennobles them. Together, they call to mind a Latin phrase very different from Malus ecclesia. E Pluribus Unum—out of many, one.

entries.title: Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’ Has a Unique Perspective on Daddy Issues
entries.summary: Elon Musk’s father, Errol Musk, agreed to be interviewed immediately.
entries.content:
Only one person agreed to be Alex Gibney’s new Elon Musk documentary immediately: Musk’s father. “We had Errol Musk at ‘hello,’” Gibney says.

Eventually, the director would speak with scores of Musk’s associates for his film. His first wife, Justine Musk, appears, as does his ex-girlfriend Ashley St. Claire. Journalist Kara Swisher, LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman, myself, and WIRED global editorial director Katie Drummond also spoke to Gibney for Musk, which hits theaters nationwide on Friday. But landing Errol Musk, with whom the Tesla and SpaceX CEO has a complicated relationship, was a watershed.

“Everybody else took a lot of persuasion,” Gibney says. “It was very difficult to get people to appear because the risk profile for talking about Musk in a way that was honest was high.”

Once Gibney interviewed all of his subjects, he had enough material to make a documentary that runs nearly four hours, including a 10-minute intermission. It’s a damning portrait of the trillionaire CEO, detailing how much of his genius is based on his formidable ability to promote his own mythology—and the stock price of his public companies.

Musk never agreed to an interview with Gibney. Instead, the director’s team researched every public comment Musk ever made and created a simulated Elon Musk who appears throughout the film.

I spoke with Gibney earlier this month about his experience making the film, why he decided to make his simulated Elon attractive, and what material he had to leave on the cutting room floor.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

ZOË SCHIFFER: Alex Gibney, thank you so much for being with us today.

ALEX GIBNEY: Good to see you, Zoë.

This shouldn’t spoil anything, but in the four years that you spent making Musk, Elon Musk never agreed to sit down with you for an interview. Instead, your team looked back through the archives of everything he has said publicly, and you put together a sort of simulated interview, which appears throughout the film as a through line. Basically, it plays into Musk’s idea that we are all, in fact, living in a simulation. How did you decide on this approach for the film?

Well, what were we gonna do? He’s the main character.

I actually thought because he’d been so outspoken about this idea of a simulation, that cinematically we should lean into that. We should play in Elon’s sandbox and have a simulated interview. As we began to develop that idea, by using his real words, his actual audio recordings, but placing them in a kind of avatar which we would design, I think there became all sorts of thematic reasons to do it.

One was because he himself had said we’re living in a simulation. But two was the importance of this notion in the Elon Musk story of the shifting sands between what is real and what is unreal. Then also, because a lot of the film deals with his issues of AI, that discomfiting relationship that we’re beginning to explore, all of us on planet Earth, with these AI LLMs and how we begin to project things on these computer interfaces, it felt like this might be something interesting to do.

By the way, you’ll notice that when Elon is talking to people in a normal interview situation, he rarely looks at the interviewer or at the camera. He’s always looking this way or that way. So we designed this in a very different way, where he’s looking right down the barrel of the lens directly at the viewer, and we thought that that would be OK. We’re gonna give Elon a break, and actually, I thought our avatar made him look pretty good compared to some of the recent images of him.

I have a question about that because your simulated Elon Musk—I think it’s fair to say—looks a lot hunkier than present day Elon Musk. He’s kind of chiseled and tan, and …

It is kind of a two-day growth of beard.

Exactly. Was that an intentional choice? And if so, can you just talk about why that was?

It was. I joke about this, but he’s the star of my movie, I want my star to look good. But I think also it would’ve been a mistake to go into slop AI territory, like some of the images that Elon’s fans are posting about me right now, to sort of denigrate him visually.

Also, to some extent, the story is also about image building, too. So I thought, “OK, let’s have some fun with that as well.” Because we had a lot of choices. I mean, we started out with the design firm, like how should he look? What should he be dressed in? You know, we put him in a gamer chair, a leather jacket. There were conscious choices.

That extends to some of the comments he makes, where I don’t find like the most bumbling comments that Elon ever made.

When we have somebody speaking about something, I want a rejoinder from Elon. We looked for the best rejoinders, like how can he come back at us? Now, later on in the film, his statements become more and more fantastical, but that also is part of what happens.

I think it really worked for the film. I’ve seen it a couple times and I think there are these famous images of Elon Musk. I’m thinking of the one where he’s on the yacht and he’s shirtless. There, it seems like if you had leaned into a less flattering image, you would’ve been playing on his turf, but in a way that would undermine the message of the movie. Whereas elevating his look allowed you to hold him quite accountable in a way that comes across pretty fair.

Yeah, we were respectful. We gave him a good look. And much better by the time we go to the archive, particularly the archive of the SpaceX IPO, when he’s begun to start looking like Kim Jong Il.

I’m curious about your thoughts on ethics. It’s not putting words in someone’s mouth, because these are all statements that Elon Musk has really made, and it’s not even like you’re particularly mashing stuff together.

But your decision, for example, to have him look right at the camera, you are making decisions for him in a way that you couldn’t with a live interview subject. So I’m just curious if you could speak to the ethical implications of that.

I think that goes to the heart of what’s different about a documentary like this and maybe a podcast interview in the sense that we’re rendering that image in a kind of broader cinematic context. The imagery itself is intended to either convey meaning or to raise questions for the viewer that they should start to think about.

As you know from being interviewed for the film, we interviewed you in front of a green screen and then placed you in a background, which we sort of reveal at different times in the movie. All of this had to do with this kind of strange unreality, real unreal world we’re living in right now.

Mm-hmm.

But also by shooting him looking into the lens I sometimes do that and I sometimes don’t. There is this interesting psychological relationship that you begin to have with a subject that I think is both real and unreal at the same time, which was part of this larger conceit in terms of trying to find a way to make the movie and the formal devices in the film itself reflect some of the thematic concerns.

Right. It also makes him feel like there is a fair amount of conviction behind what he’s saying, and there’s this relationship between him and the audience.

I feel like over the course of his public life, he doesn’t appear to have had an allegiance or ideology to one coherent political identity or to even his colleagues or close friends. These things are shifting and changing. So I am curious how that kind of came up for you in the making of the film of wanting to convey an Elon Musk in the simulated interview that represented, to the best of your ability, the quote-unquote, “true Elon.”

I mean, it’s a shape-shifting image and one which is, after all, confected, which is useful, particularly when you’re using it as a vehicle to put these statements in. I agree with your point that you just made about Elon’s ideology. I think there are a lot of wise and very perceptive books that have been written that in my view sometimes make one kind of critical flaw. They try to render a coherence about Elon’s thinking that I’m not sure is there. I think he’s far more of an improviser and shape-shifter. He has an image of himself that he wants to convey, but he’ll sculpt and change that image according to conditions and evidence, like the way he acted with Obama versus the way he acted with Trump.

I mean, there was a history there, but still they’re both serving the same purpose for him, which is, “How do I cadge the most amount of resources out of the federal government?”

I’ve thought about this a fair amount as well. I think his acquisition of Twitter now acts as a very clear example where in the moment it was clearly this impulsive decision, but now that it’s become this big source of political power for him, there’s this tendency to be like, “Oh, he was playing a complicated game all along.”

My view has always been that if Elon has a superpower it’s that he has a pretty high risk tolerance, and so he’s able to make impulsive, rash decisions and then deal with the fallout in a way that a slightly more cautious person might not be able to, for better or often worse.

He’s so comfortable with risk. It’s as though he goes through life on a canoe moving down the rapids. When he sees a rock there, he goes this way. He sees another rock or a shifting current, he goes that way. In the case of Twitter, as you pointed out in your book, he kind of bought the company on a dare, and he grossly overpaid for it and also abandoned all due diligence.

From the standpoint of a businessman, it was just dumb. But he didn’t care, and he had so many resources, what did it matter? Twitter, now X, was always a vehicle for his ambitions and his ability to court retail investors.

I don’t think it occurred to him until later when he had virtually destroyed the value of the company for the rest of us, that actually this would be a good propaganda platform for me. That’s what it becomes. Then suddenly it actually has enormous political and economic utility in a way that I don’t think he thought through at the beginning.

So Musk aside, plenty of people did speak to you for this film: Musk’s first wife, Justine; his former girlfriend, the influencer Ashley St. Clair, who he has a kid with; his father; former business partners; former colleagues; people he’s fired; the former ambassador to the United Nations, Samantha Power; Kara Swisher.

Walk me through the process of getting these people to say yes, to trust you. Specifically, was there anyone who really surprised you in their immediate willingness to say yes, and anyone who really needed extra time and conversation with you in order to be able to say yes?

Almost everybody who appeared in this film needed time to be able to process and accept appearing, in part because there was a sense of risk associated with it. Only one person agreed immediately, and that was Errol Musk.

Oh my gosh.

It was almost like, what’s that line from that great film “You had me at …”

“You had me at ‘hello.’”

We had Errol Musk at hello. “Hello, Errol, would you like to appear in this documentary?” “Yes.” We quickly rushed a crew over to his house. I did a remote interview in South Africa. It was the one interview we did that was not green screen, and he was remarkably revealing, sometimes in intended and sometimes in unintended ways.

Everybody else took a lot of persuasion. I was having conversations with Justine for over a year, I think, before she agreed to sit down. Even somebody as powerful as Reid Hoffman, same thing. So it was very difficult to get people to appear because Musk’s—the risk profile for talking about Musk in a way that was honest was high.

In some cases I did talk to a lot of people, sort of powerful people in Silicon Valley, on background—some of whom had fond feelings toward Elon and some who didn’t. I found it interesting that there’s sort of like talking to people in a gentleman’s club, and one doesn’t talk about other people publicly.

While I did learn things when they were talking to me on background or off the record, I found that kind of revolting in a way. It’s like we’re dealing with a figure now who has enormous sway over all of us, and isn’t it important to weigh in on that kind of public debate?

But that wasn’t the view that they had. In fact, there’s a guy I know who is friends with Elon and treasures his friendship with Elon, and I said, “Let’s have a conversation off the record. You know, tell me what’s great about Elon and why you like him so much.” He said “I would never betray a friend like that.”

I got that for my book as well. I don’t feel as surprised. I think if we were talking about six, seven, eight, nine, 10 years ago, like, yes. But these are similar people to those who are flying to Washington, DC to pay fealty to Trump, and going directly against values that they were talking about not that long ago.

That’s right.

I do wanna talk about Errol Musk because you brought him up. There’s this very powerful interview in the film where he talks about his son. He seems to have had a very big impact on Elon Musk’s life, and not necessarily a positive one. This was kind of the central thesis of Walter Isaacson’s biography of Elon Musk.

It kind of came down to daddy issues. So I’m curious to get your perspective on Errol’s influence on Elon and how you balanced showing the hardship of his childhood without using that as an overly simplistic explanation for his behavior today.

I think that’s an important point. I do think that Errol Musk had a powerful impact on Elon, because of how Elon felt he was treated by his dad, sometimes cruelly, psychologically. We don’t know of any kind of physical abuse. But also I think, you know, by watching Errol, you grok—to use a term from the Heinlein book—the notion that the apple doesn’t fall far from the tree.

There’s an element you can see the character of Elon. We kept it in a kind of short contained section and as an element of how we can think about Elon Musk. But I think the Walter Isaacson conclusion, in a way, is a little bit too easy. There are a lot of people who’ve been bullied or abused by their parents who don’t end up becoming bullies or abusers.

And to say it’s a kind of a mechanical thing that happens is kind of letting Elon Musk off the moral hook. That was an issue I had with Walter’s book. To some extent, we’re all grateful for the fact that he was able to spend so much time with Elon. There’s an accretion of detail in the book that’s valuable.

But I think the conclusions were sort of a get out of jail free card for the performative cruelty that ultimately he engaged in. Yet you need to know about the origin story without—it can be an explanation without being an excuse, I guess is what I would say.

I would imagine that in the making of a film like this, there is an open question at the beginning in particular about whether you’re actually going to get enough access for this to work. It’s certainly a question with features that we write. I’m curious if there was a particular interview, maybe with someone close to him, where you knew like, “OK, we’re, we’re gonna be able to do this. I think we’re gonna have enough.”

Well, weirdly, it didn’t happen until very late, and I would say it was the Justine Musk interview. I mean, the Ashley St. Clair interview is powerful as it is, and it is powerful, and it gives you a front-row seat to the election of 2024. The Justine Musk interview gave me insights into his personality that were very powerful in both understanding him as a person, but also understanding some of what he did thematically.

Because I asked her—and this answer is not in the film, but it helped to guide me—“What was it that attracted you about him back in college?” They met in college in Canada. And she said it was his enormous confidence. And then the other thing she said that’s powerful that is in the film is that she learned about gaslighting from Elon Musk.

That gaslighting thing, the idea of trying to convince somebody that the truth is other than what it is, and to suggest that you’re crazy and if you don’t go along, is a super important insight into who Elon is. And confidence, of course, is what allows that to happen.

Justine’s was such a powerful interview in the film. There are multiple moments where she cries or is near tears. She comes across as just so genuine, and I think she also seems like someone who doesn’t appear to be in it for attention or power or money. Like, there’s a point in the film where I think she says, “I really wanted to have a say in how this story was told.”

I’m thinking specifically of when their first child died in a SIDS-related incident, and Elon Musk tweets that he was holding the child. The child died in his arms. And Justine says, “No, this was one of the most defining moments of my life. He died in my arms.” You really just see how Elon has hurt her over the years.

That’s right. That gets me kind of emotionally worked up even as I think about it, because of course that moment was deeply painful for Elon, which is what Walter Isaacson spent some time on in the book. But to credit-grab in the midst of a tragedy like that seems so petulant and small and, you know, talk about main character syndrome.

One of the defining things about Elon Musk is that over time, as he increased more and more power, there was only one character in all his companies, and that’s Elon Musk, and only one character in all of his marriages. That’s Elon Musk. Everyone else recedes into the background. It’s interesting.

Justine is a storyteller. She’s a talented novelist. I went deep into reading her blogs and also the article that she wrote for Marie Claire. You know, her ability to be a storyteller is actually quite profound precisely because she’s reaching for a deeper truth.

I think when Elon is a storyteller, he’s actually reaching for fiction. He’s reaching to mythologize in a way that undoes the truth, that steers us away from that kind of hard work of getting to the stuff that is really deep and painful because it’s true.

I am curious about your take on this because it’s a question that I have had about Elon Musk: Does he actually believe what he’s saying or is he knowingly lying?

I think it’s closer to the former, and I’ve dealt with a number of characters who are like this. Sam Harris in the film makes a distinction between liars and bullshitters, and liars, of course, have to assiduously keep track of the truth in order to know when and how they’re lying.

Bullshitters just say what comes to their mind. It’s a kind of—it’s on the right track, but sort of insufficient. I think for somebody like Elon Musk—or people in the past like that I’ve dealt with, like Elizabeth Holmes or the guys at Enron or even somebody like Lance Armstrong—in the moment, because you feel a kind of righteousness about your cause, you feel you’re kind of entitled to make things up, You feel over time so entitled and so corrupted by this notion that the end justifies the means, that some kind of psychological trick is played inside your own mind where in order to be forceful and confident about what it is you’re saying in the moment, you have to believe it.

I reckoned with that with Lance Armstrong, where he could look people in the eye at a press conference and say with great force, “How dare you say that I, as a cancer survivor, would ever use performance-enhancing drugs?” And then he’d get down off the podium and do a bag of blood.

But I think in the moment he did believe what he said, because that’s how you come off as being effective. You see it particularly for people who become kind of addicted to a growing power that they have, and they see that also they have an ability to convince, like Elizabeth Holmes did.

It’s a psychological quirk that kind of takes over, and it’s peculiar, but I think it’s real.

It’s so hard to remember when talking about Elon Musk that this goober in an Occupy Mars T-shirt who’s thrashing around with a chainsaw waxing poetic has had this undeniable impact on so many people’s lives and livelihoods, and a lot of that impact has been negative.

The part of your film about DOGE, Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency, which is a short-lived stint in Washington, DC where he fired, I think, 300,000 federal workers to, quote-unquote, “solve the federal deficit.” Spoiler alert, he didn’t even come close. That was probably one of the hardest moments to watch.

Samantha Power, former ambassador to the UN, spoke specifically about the lives lost, thousands and thousands, and millions more projected, after he shuttered USAID. I’m curious, given all you know about Elon Musk at this point, and the reporting you did on DOGE, what do you think that period and that experiment was really about for him?

It wasn’t about waste, fraud, and abuse. There was an aspect of glee and performative cruelty that we tried to represent in the film by showing the DOGE cuts as a kind of first-person shooter game, juxtaposed of course, with the sober testimony of Samantha Power, who talks about how many children died as a result.

But I think in many ways the waste, fraud, and abuse was kind of the magician’s sleight of hand to say, “This is what we’re doing.” But what he was really doing was something very self-serving, which as a big tech baron, was literally destroying the regulatory state.

If there was a lot of collateral damage, people died, disease went up, who cared? It was the destruction of the inspectors general, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. He called everything corrupt without any evidence and so forth and so on.

The other thing, and the more controversial thing, which we’re all still chasing in a way, is the fact that the DOGE boys, who were clueless about the agencies they went into, nevertheless seemed to know an awful lot about data extraction and data access.

And they were granted, according to one head of IT at a federal agency I talked to, super admin status, which you know better than I, allows them to break through all sorts of silos that are intended to be erected to either protect classified information or protect our private data.

So the DOGE boys had access to vast amounts of data that no one has ever had access to in history. All of that didn’t go unnoticed, but it was the flash over the chainsaw all of the press conferences kind of hid a lot of what was really going on, I think.

Yeah, if you’re really worried about waste, fraud, and abuse, then there’s a certain level of care that you would take in your auditing. The DOGE boys were posting on X this kind of, quote-unquote, “wall of receipts” where they would talk about contracts that they’ve slashed, not understanding that in procurement paperwork, oftentimes you’ll put the total lifetime amount that could ever be spent on a contract, which is sometimes quite different, millions of dollars different, from the actual amount that was spent.

So they were claiming savings that were nowhere close to what had actually been saved. There was another, and this is in the film as well, moment where Elon Musk was talking about how they were finding tons of people who were getting Social Security benefits who were 150 years old, not understanding that when you don’t have a birthday for someone in the Social Security system, which is built on very arcane technology, really old code, it defaults to a birthday that shows someone as 150.

Anyone who had worked in SSA would’ve been able to tell them that, but they didn’t seem, to me, to be particularly interested in the details, which again, if you’re really worried about waste, fraud, and abuse, that’s all about details.

Correct. And indeed the detail that you mentioned about Social Security was actually posted on the Social Security website. So they could’ve read the website. But it goes to this kind of performative cruelty where it almost didn’t matter to them, you know?

One of the more chilling interviews, which I got from a deposition, was with one of the DOGE boys, a kid named Nate Cavanaugh.

Mm-hmm.

The questioner asked him, “Did you not care about the lives that were being affected by all of these mass firings and, and the kind of pain and suffering that would cause?” And he said, “Well, no, because we thought it was more important to reduce the federal deficit.” Next question: “Did you reduce the federal deficit?” “No.” But, you know, for a guy who’s supposed to be such a genius, you would think there would be some analysis done.

But that parallels what happened at Twitter, as you know better than anybody. In other words, they would fire people at Twitter who had actually critical jobs, without even knowing what they did.

Ezra Klein has talked about this. I think it’s really true. Like at Twitter, when you make a rash decision or you fire people, the feedback loop with the company or social media is pretty small. You can see the effects of that pretty quickly. The site starts to get glitchy.

In government, the feedback loop is really long. You don’t get to see immediately the impact of those decisions, and to me that appears to be a large reason why the effects were just so much more devastating, and honestly, while he has admitted publicly DOGE was a failure, it seems like there was no move made to kind of correct any errors.

I think even as a failure, it was sort of an intended failure in the sense that it was an attempt to really fire cannons at the government, particularly the regulatory state, so that the castle couldn’t be repaired.

Yeah, I guess I should say the stated goal of the budget deficit was a failure, but the implicit goal was quite successful.

That’s right. It was really successful. The other thing that is so disturbing about the DOGE moment is that in a lot of cases they were literally warned about the damage that was done, and that, that was certainly the case at USAID. You can make a decision as a country that we’re not gonna give aid to developing countries anymore, but money had already been appropriated by Congress. Indeed, food had been bought to send to starving children, and in some cases, boats were literally stopped to prevent that food from going to the children, who then subsequently died while they ended up burning the food on pallets someplace, literally wasting food that had already been bought and paid for.

So the cruelty had a kind of performative quality to it, which was meant, I think, to speak to the roiling anger that Musk is so good at fomenting on X and which the MAGA movement is so good at exploiting politically.

Toward the end of the film, Geoffrey Hinton comes on and says, quote, “It’s fairly clear to me Trump is hell-bent on corrupting the midterm elections. The first thing I should say is I don’t really know.

You guys are doing a lot of interesting reporting now about where the money is going and how much of it is going to focus on negative advertising versus pro-candidate stuff. But also, what kind of stories are people particularly susceptible to? We know from years of having our data mined by Facebook and X and others that it’s really useful to know what people respond to and what people think, and you have enormous data about them, then you can message certain things in order to be able to reach those soft points psychologically.

I would have to say at this moment, because it does look like we’re not far away from the election, and it looks like it’s gonna be a blue wave. We’ll see. But if it is, my bigger concern is over a disinformation campaign, aided and abetted by Elon Musk, with massive amounts of data that would try to undermine people’s confidence that the election was free and fair.

That’s what I fear most at this moment.
